explain.what: Whether the share price is above or below its average price over the last ~10 months.
explain.why: Big funds buy and sell around this line, so being above it usually means buyers are in control. It is slow: it confirms a turn after it has happened.
explain.score: The price is above its long-run average: the long-term trend is up.

explain.what: Whether the shorter trend (last ~10 weeks) is running above or below the longer trend (last ~10 months).
explain.why: It shows whether the trend itself is turning, not just where the price is today.
explain.score: The shorter trend is above the longer one: momentum is building upward.

indicators.name: Relative strength vs peers, 3 months
indicators.measured: equal-weighted average of 3 peers over 63 trading days

explain.what: Whether the stock has done better or worse than its direct competitors over the last 3 months.
explain.why: It separates something specific to this company from a whole-industry move.
explain.score: Beating its competitors: the market is rewarding this company in particular.

indicators.name: Buying vs selling volume
indicators.measured: volume on up days ÷ down days, last 20 trading days

explain.what: Whether more shares change hands on days the price rises than on days it falls (last 20 trading days).
explain.why: Large investors leave footprints in trading volume; heavy buying days suggest they are accumulating.
explain.score: Much more trading on up days: buyers are more active than sellers.

indicators.name: Short interest trend
indicators.note: Neutral: only 0.9% of freely traded shares are sold short, below the 2% minimum for a move to count.

explain.what: How many shares are borrowed and sold by investors betting the price will fall, and whether that is growing.
explain.why: Short sellers often do deep research, so a rising number of bets against a stock is a warning worth noticing.
explain.score: Bets against the stock are steady.

indicators.name: Institutional ownership change
indicators.measured: shares added minus shares cut by institutions last quarter, as % of shares outstanding
indicators.note: Proxy: counts changes in existing positions, not new or closed ones.

explain.what: Whether professional investment firms, in total, added or cut shares last quarter.
explain.why: Shows whether the big money is moving in or out. It arrives late (filings come up to 45 days after the quarter).
explain.score: Funds were broadly steady last quarter.

indicators.name: Dollar backdrop (shared macro)
indicators.measured: the dollar index 20 trading days earlier

explain.what: Whether the US dollar has strengthened or weakened over the last month.
explain.why: A strong dollar pulls money out of riskier assets worldwide and shrinks the dollar value of overseas sales.
explain.score: The dollar has strengthened: a headwind for stocks.

indicators.name: Fed rate expectations (shared macro)
indicators.measured: net odds (cut minus rise) for the next Fed meeting, 28 days earlier
indicators.note: Now: 1% cut, 17% rise; a month ago: 4% cut, 31% rise.

explain.what: Whether markets now expect the Fed to cut or raise interest rates at its next meeting, compared with a month ago.
explain.why: Interest rates set the price of every other asset; expectations move long before the Fed acts.

indicators.name: Revenue growth trend
indicators.measured: average growth of the prior 4 quarters, each vs a year earlier

explain.what: Whether sales growth is speeding up or slowing down compared with the past year.
explain.why: The plainest evidence of whether customers want more of what the company sells.

indicators.name: Gross margin trend
indicators.measured: gross margin of the 4 quarters a year earlier

explain.what: Whether the share of each sales dollar kept as gross profit is rising or falling.
explain.why: A company that can hold or raise its margins has pricing power, a sign of strong demand.

indicators.name: Earnings forecast revisions
indicators.measured: consensus EPS for the year to 2028-06-30, 90 days earlier

explain.what: Whether analysts have raised or cut their profit forecasts over the last 3 months.
explain.why: Changes in expected profit are one of the most reliable drivers of share prices over the following months.
explain.score: Analysts are raising their profit forecasts.

explain.what: Whether management's outlook for next quarter came in above or below what analysts expected.

indicators.name: Forward P/E vs peers

indicators.note: Next 12 months: blends consensus EPS for the years to 2027-06-30 and 2028-06-30 ($20.82). Yahoo's next-fiscal-year figure: 22.4x.

explain.what: How much investors pay for each dollar of the company's expected profit, compared with its competitors.
explain.why: Paying much more than for rivals means good news is already in the price, so there is less room for disappointment.
explain.score: Priced roughly in line with its competitors.

explain.what: The same comparison as above, but allowing for how fast profits are expected to grow.
explain.why: A higher price can be fair if profits grow faster; this checks whether they do.
explain.score: Still expensive after allowing for its expected growth.

indicators.name: EV/EBITDA vs peers
indicators.note: EV = market value + debt − cash ($3,982bn) ÷ last-12-month EBITDA ($194.2bn).

explain.what: The company's total value (including debt) compared with its operating profit, against competitors.
explain.why: Unlike the P/E, this counts debt, so an indebted company cannot look artificially cheap.
explain.score: In line with its competitors once debt is counted.

indicators.name: P/E vs own 5-year history
indicators.measured: the stock's own median trailing P/E, last 5 years (weekly)
indicators.note: Trailing (last 12 months actual) P/E: free forward P/E history is too short.

explain.what: How much investors pay for each dollar of profit today, compared with this company's own usual level over 5 years.
explain.why: Shows whether the stock is cheap or expensive by its own standards, which catches whole-industry re-pricing.

past.date: Wed 29 Jul 2026, after the US close (Thu 30 Jul, about 4am Singapore)
past.vs: Revenue $90.0bn, +18% vs a year earlier, vs $87.6bn consensus (Reuters/Visible Alpha): +2.7% beat. EPS $4.81 reported; $4.74 excluding OpenAI vs $4.24 expected (+11.8%). Azure +43% (also +43% excluding currency) vs about 40% expected and Microsoft's own 39-40% guide.
past.guide: September quarter: revenue $89.85-90.95bn (+15.7% to +17.1% vs $77.7bn a year earlier; midpoint +16.4%) vs about $89.7bn consensus (+15.5%); Azure about +45% in constant currency vs about 41% expected.
past.reaction: Shares +15.5% on 30 Jul ($451.10 vs $390.54), Microsoft's biggest one-day gain since 2008 (about $450bn of market value).
take: Azure accelerated. +43% vs +40% in the March quarter and +39% in December (each vs a year earlier); guided to about +45% for September.
Still short of capacity. Demand exceeds the data-centre capacity Microsoft has; no end date given.

Capex keeps rising. $41bn in the quarter including finance leases; over $50bn guided for September. The calendar-2026 plan was cut to about $175bn from $190bn because more data-centre leases are now operating leases, which Microsoft does not count as capex; the CFO said spending plans are unchanged. Data-centre buildings are also now depreciated over 25 years instead of 15 (profit effect 'minimal', per the CFO).
Copilot is selling. Over 30m paid Microsoft 365 Copilot seats (20m+ in March); net new seats more than doubled vs the March quarter.

Backlog is OpenAI-heavy. Contracted future revenue (RPO) $678bn, +84%; excluding OpenAI +25%. OpenAI was $24.1bn of FY26 revenue, 7.3% of the total (annual report); a broker (BNP Paribas) estimates about 23% of Azure.
Margins slipping slowly. Gross margin 67.2% vs 68.6% a year earlier; FY27 operating margin guided down by less than 1 point.
Cash. Free cash flow $19.6bn in the quarter on $55.4bn operating cash flow.

mix.source: SEC filings (10-Q / 10-K inline XBRL), 8 filings; quarter 4 = full year minus the first three quarters

segments.name: Azure & server products
segments.sells: Azure cloud computing and AI capacity, plus server software (SQL Server, Windows Server) and GitHub.
segments.buyers: Companies, governments and AI labs (OpenAI the largest), mostly on pay-as-you-use or multi-year contracts.
pos: Biggest and fastest-growing part: about 39% of sales and +31% over the last 4 quarters vs the 4 quarters before (Azure alone +43% in the June quarter).
Contracted backlog of $678bn (all commercial, Jun-26) gives years of visibility.
Usage-based: grows as customers run more AI workloads, without new licence sales.
neg: Earns below the company's segment operating margin: Intelligent Cloud 41% vs about 47% for all segments (last 4 quarters), and slipping as AI capacity costs rise.
Needs about $175bn of capex in calendar 2026 (including leases); payback depends on growth staying high.
Concentrated: OpenAI was 7.3% of all FY26 revenue (annual report) and an estimated ~23% of Azure (broker estimate).

segments.name: Enterprise & partner services
segments.sells: Enterprise support contracts, consulting and partner services.
neg: Small (about 2.5% of sales) and slow-growing (+7% vs a year earlier, last 4 quarters).
Shares Intelligent Cloud's margin, which is falling.

segments.name: Microsoft 365 commercial
segments.sells: Office, Teams, Exchange, security and Copilot subscriptions sold to companies (per user, per month).
segments.buyers: Businesses and public bodies worldwide; over 30m paid Copilot seats (Jun-26).
pos: Recurring subscriptions: about 31% of sales, +16% over the last 4 quarters vs the 4 before (Microsoft 365 commercial cloud alone +14% in the June quarter, excluding currency).
Earns the highest margin: Productivity and Business Processes 60% segment operating margin (last 4 quarters), up from 58% a year earlier.
Copilot adds a price uplift on an installed base of hundreds of millions of users.
neg: Growth depends on price rises and Copilot add-ons more than new users.
AI tools from rivals (Google, Anthropic, OpenAI) threaten to change how office work is done: the Feb-26 software sell-off was about this.
Seat counts are tied to employment at customers.

segments.name: LinkedIn
segments.sells: LinkedIn premium subscriptions, recruiting tools and advertising.
pos: +11% over the last 4 quarters vs the 4 before; unique professional data.
neg: Recruiting revenue swings with the hiring cycle.
Advertising part competes with Google and Meta.

segments.name: Dynamics & Microsoft 365 consumer
segments.sells: Dynamics business software (finance, sales, customer service) and Microsoft 365 subscriptions for households.
segments.buyers: Mid-size and large companies (Dynamics); consumers (Microsoft 365 Personal/Family).
pos: Fastest growth in the Productivity segment: +19% over the last 4 quarters vs the 4 before.
neg: Dynamics competes with Salesforce, SAP and Oracle.

segments.name: Windows, Xbox, search & devices
segments.sells: Windows licences for PC makers, Surface devices, Xbox consoles, games and Game Pass, and Bing/news advertising.
segments.buyers: PC makers, consumers, gamers and advertisers.
pos: Search advertising and Windows still generate cash.
Xbox content (incl. Activision) is a large library.
neg: Shrinking: about 16% of sales vs 19% a year earlier; revenue -1% over the last 4 quarters vs the 4 before (June quarter -4%).
Lowest margin: 27% segment operating margin (last 4 quarters).
Not recurring: depends on PC and console cycles.

pos: The shift in mix alone added 0.4 pts to segment operating margin vs a year earlier (last 4 quarters vs the 4 quarters a year earlier, each part's margin held at that earlier level).
Partly recurring revenue (long-life contracts or design wins) up 5 pts in 3 years to 47% of sales (last 4 quarters).
neg: Fastest-growing part (Azure & server products, +31% vs a year earlier) earns below the company segment operating margin.

shift.title: What the shift means for Microsoft
pos: Sales are moving towards cloud and subscriptions: Azure & server products rose from about 35% to 39% of sales in a year (last 4 quarters vs the 4 a year earlier), and the low-margin personal computing segment fell from 19% to 16%.
The mix shift on its own added about 0.4 points to segment operating margin vs a year earlier, because personal computing (27% margin) shrank.
More of revenue is contracted or subscription-based, which makes earnings steadier.
